title: Day and Night 8
content:
Stepping into the room, he shut the door behind him and leaned back against the wooden frame. The moment the faint, measured click of Lan Wangji’s door closing echoed from across the hall, Wei Wuxian raised a hand and slapped himself across the face.

He slumped heavily onto the daybed, burying his blazing face in his palms. He sat there for a long time, but the heat refused to recede—neither from his cheeks nor from deep inside his veins. Grabbing the ceramic pot from the table, he doused his head and face with cold tea, but it did nothing. From head to toe, he reeked of Lan Wangji.

Wei Wuxian knew that if he stayed here, trapped with the thought of Lan Wangji just a single wall away—replaying what they had been doing only moments ago—he wouldn't find a second of peace tonight. He couldn't remain in this room. Not like this.

Pushing the window open, he stepped onto the sill and vaulted out. Like a shadow slipping through the night, he dropped soundlessly into the empty street below.

The hour was late, the cobblestones deserted, making it easy for him to break into a reckless, dead-out sprint.

He only came to a halt when he reached the whitewashed wall Lan Wangji had defaced during his drunken spree.

The plaster was covered in a mess of crude doodles: bunnies, pheasants, and clumsy stick-figure heads. Looking at them, Wei Wuxian vividly pictured Lan Wangji’s dead-serious focus while sketching each one, and the earnest way he’d dragged Wei Wuxian over to admire his handiwork. A faint, bittersweet curve tugged at the corner of his lips.

A crushing wave of regret slammed into his chest.

If only I hadn't let myself run wild on a drunken whim.

If he hadn't, he could still be playing the innocent friend, brazenly squeezing into Lan Wangji’s bed, sprawling out beside him to comfortably fake sleep or drift off in peace. He wouldn't be banished into the dead of night, tearing down empty alleys like a headless fly just to burn off the madness clawing at his chest.

Wei Wuxian reached out, his fingertips grazing the two little doodles with puckered lips sharing a kiss, before drifting up to the words scrawled above: Lan Wangji was here. The graffiti needed scraping off, but before he erased it, he let his finger trace the strokes of the name Lan Wangji.

Once. Twice. Three times.

The more he traced the characters, the harder it was to pull his hand away.

A faint rasping noise suddenly cut through the quiet. Snapping to attention, Wei Wuxian rounded the street corner, only to find a dark figure plastered against the wall. Armed with a small metal file, the figure was painstakingly scraping away the graffiti.

Wei Wuxian stood there, speechless.

Wen Ning turned around, his face powdered in white plaster dust. “Master Wei, what are you doing here?”

“What are you doing?” Wei Wuxian asked.

“Oh,” Wen Ning said simply. “I saw that Master Lan wrote so much. When the locals wake up tomorrow and see it, it might cause trouble, so I thought I’d scrape some off…” He paused, glancing around in confusion. “Where is Master Lan?”

Looking down, Wei Wuxian muttered, “He’s resting. I just came out for a walk.”

Sensing that something was terribly off, Wen Ning lowered his file. “Master Wei, did something happen?”

He took two steps closer, then froze dead in his tracks, stumbling back several paces. Wei Wuxian blinked. “What are you doing now?”

Wen Ning looked horrified, waving his hands in a frantic panic. “Nothing, nothing! It’s nothing!”

Wei Wuxian caught on immediately—the corpse was thoroughly mortified. Glancing down at himself, he noticed the faint reddish bruises ringing his wrists, left behind when Lan Wangji had pinned him to the mattress. He touched his own lips; they were still noticeably swollen. When the two of them had lost their minds rolling around the daybed, practically trying to fuse into one another, Lan Wangji had nipped and bit his way across his skin. His neck was probably a colorful disaster. If Wen Ning had a pulse, his face would have been flushed scarlet by now.

Completely at a loss, Wei Wuxian rubbed his face with a heavy sigh. “You… ah, forget it.”

He slid down against the brick corner and sat flat on the ground. “I want a drink.”

Wen Ning piped up instantly, “I’ll go buy some.”

“Get back here!” Wei Wuxian snapped. “Where do you think you’re running off to?”

Wen Ning shuffled back, sheepish. “To find wine…”

“I swear, you…” Wei Wuxian shook his head. “I just threw that out casually. You don't actually have to hunt down liquor for me—you’re not my servant.”

“I know,” Wen Ning murmured.

“Besides, do you even have money?”

“No…”

“See? Exactly what I thought!”

Wen Ning’s voice dipped into quiet envy: “Master Lan always carries so much… so much silver on him. It must be nice.”

Wei Wuxian leaned his head back, thumping it against the wall several times with a string of drawn-out groans. “Forget it. I’m done. I'm never touching liquor again.”

Wen Ning blinked in shock. “Why?”

“Alcohol ruins lives,” Wei Wuxian grumbled. “I’m quitting.”

The corner of Wen Ning’s mouth twitched faintly. Wei Wuxian narrowed his eyes. “What’s that face for? You don't believe me?”

Wen Ning stammered, “No, no… it’s just… back then, didn't my sister try everything under the sun, and she still couldn't make you quit…?”

Wei Wuxian barked a laugh. “Haha, right. Her ‘methods’ amounted to poking me full of acupuncture needles every two or three days.”

Once the laughter faded, Wei Wuxian’s expression sobered. “Wen Ning, have you ever thought about what you’re going to do once all this mess is finally over?”

Wen Ning went still. “What I’m going to do?”

In this world, Wen Ning had no family left—hardly even an acquaintance to his name. He had never been good at making his own decisions, lacking the resolve to chart his own course. He had spent his life either trailing behind Wen Qing or following behind Wei Wuxian; beyond that, he likely had no idea where to go, or where he even belonged. Yet Wei Wuxian still hoped he would find a path of his own. But spelling it out felt too much like driving him away.

Then again, if Wen Ning didn't know where to go, did Wei Wuxian have any better clue? While traveling alongside Lan Wangji, the thought had never crossed his mind; he had simply taken it for granted that things would stay that way forever. But after tonight, their bond might never recover. Wandering the four seas alone, drifting wherever the wind took him—surely that was an option.

Yet a voice deep inside told him plainly: No, it isn't.

The absurd, shameless claim he had blurted out to Jin Ling on Koi Tower—meeting Hanguang-jun changed everything. I can't live without him now. I don't want anyone in this world except my Hanguang-jun—had come back to bite him in the end: as it turned out, the present Wei Wuxian truly couldn't survive without Lan Wangji.

Letting out a long, hollow breath, Wei Wuxian groaned, “I really need a damn drink.”

The more he brooded, the more suffocating the misery became. The restless anxiety bottled up in his chest finally detonated into pure, reckless irritation. He sprang to his feet. “Screw it. Wen Ning, move!”

Wen Ning scrambled up. “Where are we going?”

Wei Wuxian cracked his knuckles, a grim edge to his smirk. “To fuck some shit up.”
